analysis.one_liner: Requires 100% renewable electricity, zero-emission car sales, and regenerative farming on big agribusiness by 2030.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in three House committees without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended, with 13 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forced a rapid national shift to clean energy and farming: by 2030, all electricity sold by larger retail suppliers would have to come from renewable sources, every new car and truck sold by manufacturers would have to be zero-emission, and large publicly traded farm and livestock companies would have to use regenerative farming practices and meet animal welfare rules. To ease the transition, it offers grants covering up to half the cost and lets qualifying businesses double certain tax deductions. It never received any committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: Households exposed to air pollution and climate-driven disasters, since electricity, transportation, and agriculture account for over 60% of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions. Also renewable energy manufacturers, electric vehicle makers, and farmers using regenerative practices, who would gain customers and markets.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to pollution and climate disasters

how_it_helps.text: Requires 80% renewable electricity by 2027 and 100% by 2030 for retail electric suppliers selling at least 1,000 megawatt-hours a year [S3].
Requires 80% of new vehicles sold by manufacturers to be zero-emission by 2027 and 100% by 2030, added to the Clean Air Act [S3].
Requires large publicly traded land and livestock corporations to manage 50% of land and livestock regeneratively by 2025-26, 75% by 2027-29, and 100% by 2030 [S3].
Creates competitive grants covering up to 50% of transition costs for electric suppliers, vehicle manufacturers, and covered farm corporations [S3].
Lets eligible businesses double tax deductions for qualified climate transition costs and use accelerated expensing for transition property [S3].

Directs USDA to issue animal welfare rules banning routine antibiotics and hormones, physical mutilations like debeaking, and confinement feeding operations, with public livestream access after violations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Fossil-fuel power suppliers, conventional vehicle manufacturers, and large agribusiness corporations bear the cost of converting operations by fixed deadlines, softened by grants and tax breaks. Taxpayers bear the grant and tax expenditures. Consumers could face some of the transition costs passed through utility and vehicle prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil utilities, automakers, agribusiness, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The deadlines are aggressive: 80% renewable electricity and zero-emission vehicle sales by 2027 would require rebuilding power generation and supply chains within a few years of enactment, and grants depend on annual appropriations that Congress may not provide [S3].

The clean-technology transition relies on mined materials and manufacturing at a scale the bill acknowledges by directing DOE to write rules to eliminate rare earth metals and ensure recycling, a problem it mandates but does not itself solve [S3].
Doubling tax deductions and allowing expensing for transition property reduces federal revenue, so taxpayers absorb part of the cost even beyond the grants [S3].

Regenerative farming and animal welfare mandates apply to corporations that contract with independent farmers and ranchers, whose operations and incomes could be squeezed by compliance demands set by the companies they supply [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims at the largest sources of U.S. emissions with enforceable deadlines and real money to help covered businesses comply. Its weakness is feasibility: the timelines are compressed, funding is not guaranteed, and the burden on contract farmers is unaddressed. Even sympathetic readers would call the deadlines aspirational rather than fully costed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and to two Agriculture subcommittees a month later, but no committee ever held a hearing or markup, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Adriano Espaillat introduced the bill on January 27, 2023, with four original cosponsors, and it was referred to the Agriculture, Ways and Means, and Energy and Commerce Committees [S1][S3][S5].

On February 23, 2023, it was referred to the Agriculture Subcommittee on Conservation, Research, and Biotechnology and the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry; those were its last recorded actions [S5].
It attracted 13 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never advanced to a floor vote in either chamber [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil-fuel power suppliers, conventional automakers, and large agribusiness are better off because the bill died: none of the 2027-2030 mandates, emission rules, or animal welfare requirements will take effect, and the status quo continues.

for.name: Adriano Espaillat

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were House Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican supported the bill at any point, and the Republican-held committees took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill requires 80% renewable electricity by 2027 and 100% by 2030, forcing replacement of fossil generation. Its interest in blocking the bill ran against the public's interest in lower emissions, though its opposition was passive since the bill never got a hearing.
The bill mandates 100% zero-emission vehicle sales by 2030 but pays up to half the transition cost through grants and doubled tax deductions. Stopping it preserved the gasoline vehicle business.

Publicly traded farm and livestock companies face regenerative farming quotas, greenhouse gas reduction rules, and animal welfare mandates, offset by 50% cost-share grants. Stopping the bill left intensive confinement operations and routine antibiotic and hormone use untouched.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and clean technology manufacturers
industries.note: A 100% renewable electricity standard and zero-emission vehicle mandate would create guaranteed demand for wind, solar, storage, and EV production. The bill's loss left their market opportunity unrealized.
Regenerative practice mandates for large corporations, reduced synthetic fertilizer use, and pasture requirements would expand markets for farmers already using these methods.
